title: Sore Throat / Pharyngitis Differential Diagnosis
description: Differential diagnosis for acute sore throat (pharyngitis) in adolescents and adults, covering infectious (viral, bacterial, fungal) and non-infectious etiologies, with emphasis on identifying Group A Streptococcal pharyngitis and life-threatening complications.
source_description: Shulman ST, Bisno AL, Clegg HW, et al. Clinical Practice Guideline for the Diagnosis and Management of Group A Streptococcal Pharyngitis: 2012 Update by the Infectious Diseases Society of America. Clin Infect Dis 2012;55(10):e86-e102.

diagnoses.name: Epiglottitis
key_features: Severe sore throat with relatively normal-appearing oropharynx
Tripod positioning / preference to sit upright
recommended_tests: Lateral soft tissue neck X-ray (thumbprint sign)

diagnoses.name: Peritonsillar Abscess
key_features: Uvular deviation away from affected side
red_flags: Extension to deep neck space (torticollis, neck swelling)
recommended_tests: CT neck with contrast if deep space extension suspected

diagnoses.name: Retropharyngeal Abscess
recommended_tests: Lateral soft tissue neck X-ray (widened prevertebral space)

diagnoses.name: Lemierre Syndrome (Septic Jugular Thrombophlebitis)
key_features: Sore throat followed by high spiking fevers and rigors
Lateral neck pain, swelling, or tenderness along sternocleidomastoid
Worsening symptoms days after initial pharyngitis
red_flags: Persistent or worsening fever despite antibiotics
recommended_tests: CT neck with contrast (internal jugular vein thrombosis)
CT chest if pulmonary emboli suspected

diagnoses.name: Group A Streptococcal (GAS) Pharyngitis
key_features: Absence of cough, rhinorrhea, or conjunctivitis
red_flags: Signs of suppurative complications (peritonsillar abscess, neck swelling)
Scarlet fever rash with systemic toxicity
recommended_tests: Throat culture (if RADT negative in children/adolescents)

diagnoses.name: Viral Pharyngitis (Rhinovirus, Adenovirus, Coronavirus, Parainfluenza, Influenza)
key_features: Concurrent cough, rhinorrhea, or nasal congestion
recommended_tests: Influenza rapid test if suspected during flu season

diagnoses.name: Fusobacterium necrophorum Pharyngitis (Non-Lemierre)
key_features: Acute onset sore throat with exudates
Negative rapid strep test and throat culture
More common in adolescents and young adults
red_flags: Persistent or worsening symptoms after 5-7 days (risk of Lemierre syndrome)
recommended_tests: Throat culture (not routinely detected on standard culture)

diagnoses.name: Gonococcal Pharyngitis
key_features: Often asymptomatic or mild sore throat
red_flags: Disseminated gonococcal infection (arthritis, skin lesions, fever)
recommended_tests: Pharyngeal nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT) for N. gonorrhoeae
Concurrent testing for Chlamydia and HIV

diagnoses.name: Oropharyngeal Candidiasis (Thrush)
key_features: Sore throat with white curd-like plaques on mucosa
Plaques can be scraped off leaving erythematous base
red_flags: New oral candidiasis in a patient without known risk factors (consider HIV testing)
recommended_tests: HIV testing if no other risk factor identified

diagnoses.name: Allergic or Irritant Pharyngitis
key_features: Dry or scratchy throat, especially in morning
Exposure to allergens, smoke, or dry air
recommended_tests: Trial of antihistamine or nasal corticosteroid

diagnoses.name: Gastroesophageal Reflux (GERD)-Related Pharyngitis
key_features: Chronic sore throat worse in morning

also_consider.name: Acute HIV Infection (Acute Retroviral Syndrome)
also_consider.rationale: Pharyngitis with fever, rash, and lymphadenopathy 2-4 weeks after exposure; always consider in sexually active patients with mononucleosis-like illness and negative Monospot

also_consider.name: Herpangina (Coxsackievirus)
also_consider.rationale: Vesicles and ulcers on posterior pharynx and soft palate; more common in children but occurs in adults, especially in summer/fall

also_consider.name: Herpes Simplex Pharyngitis
also_consider.rationale: Vesicles and shallow ulcers on anterior mouth and pharynx; consider in immunocompromised patients or with primary HSV infection

also_consider.name: Diphtheria
also_consider.rationale: Gray-white pharyngeal membrane that bleeds when removed; rare in vaccinated populations but must be considered in unvaccinated or travelers from endemic areas

also_consider.name: Ludwig Angina (Submandibular Space Infection)
also_consider.rationale: Floor of mouth swelling and elevation of tongue with throat pain; usually odontogenic origin, can compromise airway rapidly

also_consider.name: Kawasaki Disease
also_consider.rationale: Pharyngeal erythema with fever, conjunctivitis, rash, and extremity changes in children under 5; incomplete forms can present primarily with pharyngitis

also_consider.name: Arcanobacterium haemolyticum Pharyngitis
also_consider.rationale: Scarlatiniform rash with pharyngitis in adolescents/young adults; can mimic GAS pharyngitis and is not detected on standard RADT

also_consider.name: Head and Neck Malignancy
also_consider.rationale: Persistent unilateral sore throat, dysphagia, or neck mass in adults over 50; always consider in smokers or heavy alcohol users with symptoms lasting more than 2 weeks

also_consider.name: Thyroiditis (Subacute/De Quervain)
also_consider.rationale: Anterior neck pain radiating to throat and jaw, often following viral URI; tender thyroid on palpation with possible thyrotoxicosis symptoms

also_consider.name: Aphthous Stomatitis
also_consider.rationale: Recurrent painful shallow ulcers on non-keratinized oral mucosa; sore throat when lesions affect posterior pharynx

clinical_reasoning_prompt: This is an evidence-based reference set, not an exhaustive differential. Viral pharyngitis accounts for the majority (50-80%) of sore throat presentations, but the critical clinical task is to identify GAS pharyngitis (to prevent rheumatic fever) and to recognize life-threatening complications such as deep neck space infections, epiglottitis, and Lemierre syndrome. Use the Centor/McIsaac score to guide testing decisions for GAS. Consider atypical presentations, immunocompromised status, sexual history, travel history, and vaccination status. Persistent unilateral symptoms or failure to improve should prompt re-evaluation for suppurative complications or alternative diagnoses.
